newsitem.title: ITALY: Death penalty foes thank U.S. court for stay.
newsitem.headline: Death penalty foes thank U.S. court for stay.

text.p: Joyous opponents of the death penalty held placards saying "Thank You" at a candlelight rally at the American embassy in Rome after the U.S. Supreme Court blocked the execution of a death-row inmate on Tuesday.
"This is great news," said Cosetta Campello, 28, as she held an American flag in one hand and a lighted candle in another. A placard saying "Grazie" (Thank You) hung from her neck.
"This is just the start. Now we have to help convince America, which defines itself as a democratic country, that it has to abolish the death penalty."
Campello was one of 100 people, including several members of parliament, who demonstrated in front of the U.S. embassy on Rome's famed Via Veneto.
Joseph O'Dell, convicted of the rape and murder in 1985 of 44-year-old secretary Helen Schartner, had been due to die by lethal injection in Virginia on Wednesday.

His case, which has received very little attention in the United States, has been a major story in Italy, where it brought pleas for clemency from Pope John Paul, President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro and Prime Minister Romano Prodi.
The death penalty for civilians is against the law in Italy and Italians are in the forefront of international campaigns to abolish capital punishment.

Vatican spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls expressed "satisfaction" over the decision. He stressed that the Pope's mercy pleas were not an attempt to take sides on O'Dell's guilt or innocence but to defend human life.
Deputies in Italy's lower house of parliament interrupted a debate to applaud the Supreme Court's decision.
O'Dell and his supporters say that post-trial DNA testing shows that blood stains on his clothing do not match the victim's and want the case re-opened.
O'Dell's lawyers made the appeal to the Supreme Court after the new DNA evidence was ruled out by judges because it was submitted past a deadline.
The Supreme Court granted a temporary stay of execution that will remain in effect until it acts on the appeal challenging his conviction and sentence.
The Rome vigil had been planned before news of the court's decision reached Italy.
Demonstrators hastily prepared the "Thank You" placards and a U.S. flag that had been brought to the embassy as a target of comtempt was instead waved with joy.
While the demonstrators expressed gratitude to the court for temporarily blocking the execution, they said they were determined to continue their campaign to ban capital punishment.
"We have only won time. We don't know what will happen next," said Sergio D'Elia, secretary of the anti-death penalty organisation Hands Off Cain.
"But at least the court has confirmed the right of every condemned man to prove his innocence," he said.
The demonstrators, who held up a yellow banner reading "Clinton: Abolish the Death Penalty," said the role of the Pope in drawing attention to the case may have been decisive.
"The Pope helped us to break down that wall of silence and helped us to gain time," said D'Elia. "For that we are very grateful".
